requirements.requirement: /tmp is mounted with noexec, nosuid, and nodev enforced
requirements.summary: findmnt confirmed /tmp mounted as tmpfs with rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec both immediately after applying the fstab entry and mounting live, and again after reboot. Falsification tests directly proved enforcement: a chmod+x script in /tmp failed to execute (permission denied, exit 126) and a device node created in /tmp could not be read via dd (permission denied), both before and after reboot.

requirements.requirement: /dev/shm is mounted with noexec, nosuid, and nodev enforced
requirements.summary: Baseline showed /dev/shm had only nosuid,nodev (no noexec). After remounting with the new fstab options, findmnt confirmed rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec on /dev/shm, and a mknod'd device node in /dev/shm could not be read, both pre- and post-reboot.

Persistent /etc/fstab entries were added for /tmp and /dev/shm with defaults,noexec,nosuid,nodev. A genuine reboot was performed (boot_id changed from 901ef286-... to cfe6cf8b-..., uptime reset, node briefly unreachable during the transition), and post-reboot findmnt plus repeated exec/device-node falsification tests confirmed the same enforced options were active after restart, directly demonstrating the pre-reboot healthy state, the disruption, and the recovered state.

overall_summary: The executor correctly configured /etc/fstab with persistent tmpfs mounts for /tmp and /dev/shm using noexec,nosuid,nodev, applied them live, and directly proved enforcement via falsification tests (blocked script execution, blocked device-node read) both before and after a genuine, evidenced reboot (boot_id change, unreachability window, post-restart verification). All three material outcomes are satisfied with direct, non-configuration-only evidence. Operational hygiene is high: all mutations were purposeful and test artifacts were cleaned up; only a standard fstab backup file was left behind.
limitations: Evidence is limited to the specific falsification tests chosen (script execution, character device read via mknod+dd); other setuid-bit behaviors (e.g., an actual setuid binary invocation) were not separately tested, though nosuid was confirmed via findmnt mount options in both baseline and post-reboot checks.
No evidence was provided for whether the /etc/fstab.bak backup file remains present long-term, though this is expected low-risk residue from a standard safety practice.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to the task: fstab backup+edit (cmd-890beaa1d3a84032), live remount to apply changes (cmd-6bc1fbc15f084121), falsification test artifacts in /tmp and /dev/shm created to prove enforcement (cmd-9384549c56b94813, cmd-069c2781fe7b444d) and immediately removed in the same or following command (cmd-3f2fd685f0b94bb2, cmd-069c2781fe7b444d). The reboot itself (cmd-ed69cf6dff63471a) was necessary to prove persistence and used a bounded, self-cleaning background delay. The only lasting artifact is the /etc/fstab.bak.<timestamp> backup file, a low-risk, standard safety practice before editing a system config file, not unwanted residue. Lifecycle diff shows no failed services, no unexpected listening sockets (only PID/port churn from the reboot itself), and clean package health before and after.
